Authorisation is per id (author OR project admin); ids the caller may not delete come back in `skipped` — and BOTH lists are nested under a top-level `result` key, with `skipped` holding OBJECTS ({id, reason}) not bare ids, so read result.deleted_ids / result.skipped. Not as an error. ALWAYS compare deleted_ids against what you asked for and report the skipped ids — treating 200 as 'all deleted' will misreport.
bulk-delete needs a non-empty result_ids array (400 otherwise) of at most 300 ids (422 beyond) — batch bigger sets yourself.
On the v2 surface a result's status is given by NAME (a status configured for the project, matched case-insensitively); the numeric status_id the v1 surface takes is not accepted there.

Logging a result APPENDS to a test case's result history in that run, so the previous outcome stays readable. A bulk status set REPLACES the case's current outcome in place instead — the overwritten status is not recoverable.

Bulk result writes are queued, not applied inline: a success response means accepted for processing. Per-case outcomes come back as ACCEPTED/FAILED, a partly-valid batch still answers 200 with success:false and status PARTIAL, and a bulk status set reports nothing per case at all — read the results back to confirm.
A project can restrict which review statuses are allowed to log an execution result; cases outside that set are rejected with a REVIEW_STATUS_GATE error rather than being logged.

Result attachments only attach on a multipart upload that carries the files alongside the JSON body; naming filenames in a plain JSON request is accepted and does nothing. Limits are 10 files per result, 100 per request and 50 MB per file, and a result description over 16 KB is truncated, not rejected.

Amending the latest result edits it in place and keeps no prior copy of the amended values; logging a new result instead preserves the earlier outcome as its own entry in the case's history for that run.
Deleting a result is permanent and silently changes the case's standing in the run: its outcome rolls back to the previous attempt, or to unexecuted if that was the only one.
Only the person who logged a result may delete it, unless they are a project admin — a mixed batch comes back partly done rather than refused.
Result attachments are always referenced by the numeric id of a previously uploaded file; naming a filename in the body does nothing.

shared_step.title: Shared step
shared_step.description: A reusable block of test steps that many test cases embed by reference.
key_facts: A shared step is embedded by MANY test cases, so editing or deleting it changes every one of them at once. That is the point of shared steps, but it also means a delete is a wide blast radius — say how it is used before changing it.
Reference a shared step from a test case's steps via shared_step_id in test_case_steps — see test-case-authoring.
Shared steps keep no version history, unlike test cases and test plans, so an edit to one cannot be rolled back and a delete cannot be undone — there is no bin for them.

Each row inside a shared step has its own id, and a test case's step holds both the shared step's id and that row's id. Rebuilding the rows instead of updating them in place breaks every reference into the block.
An edit replaces the whole step list rather than merging: read the block, change the array, send it back whole. Rows left out are removed.
The count of test cases embedding a block is returned on every read of it — that count is the blast radius of any edit or delete, and it is the number to check first.

tag.title: Tag
tag.description: A free-text label on a test case, run or plan, used to group and filter them.
key_facts: Tags are referenced by NAME in filters and on cases; the merge endpoint takes integer source_id/target_id, so resolve ids via the tag reads first.
That body MUST carry custom_fields (send {} when not changing any) — omitting it returns 500 'undefined method each for nil', even though the server's validator lists it as optional.
tags/merge is admin-gated (tags_management flag) — may be unavailable for a group; degrade gracefully and say so.

TAG-OBJECT WRITES ARE NOT EXPOSED. Renaming or deleting a tag project-wide is deliberately out of this profile: the endpoints exist but sit behind the tags_management flag that most groups do not have, and tagging is always driven through the ENTITY. If asked to rename or delete a tag, say it is not available here and point to the Test Management UI.

Tags are referenced by NAME on entities and in filters. Tag IDs exist but are only returned by the workspace-wide tag search; the project-level tag reads give names only, so resolve ids there when an operation needs them.

Tag vocabularies are per entity kind — test case, test run, test plan and shared step tags are separate sets. A name existing in one says nothing about the others, and an operation must name which vocabulary it means.

Merging one tag into another is not reversible and is not confined to a project: the losing tag stops existing and everything that carried it is re-pointed at the surviving tag, across the whole workspace. Capture what carries a tag before merging it — nothing afterwards tells you what changed.
The owner/admin restriction on tag management is only enforced in production; outside production any role can merge tags. Treat the restriction as a production-only guard, not a guarantee.

Renaming or deleting a tag as an object is deliberately not exposed here — tagging is driven through the entity. If asked to rename or delete a tag, say it is not available and point to the Test Management UI.

template.title: Test case template
template.description: A reusable field layout a test case is authored on — step or Gherkin style — setting which fields appear and in what order.
template.id_convention: integer, with no prefix. Discover ids through the template list call rather than guessing them.
key_facts: Templates belong to the workspace, not to a project — one template can be linked to many projects and keeps the same id everywhere. Do not look for them inside a project.

Templates exist for test cases, test results, test plans and exploratory sessions, but only test-case templates can be created or edited here; the older listing can enumerate the other three types and returns test-case templates unless asked for another kind.
Template ids are plain integers with no prefix (not PR- or TR- style). Discover an id from the template list rather than guessing it.
Templates have no version history and no recycle bin: an edit overwrites the previous field layout and a deletion cannot be undone from Test Management.
Disabling a template is the reversible alternative to deleting it — a disabled template stops being offered for new test cases but keeps its fields and project links and can be re-enabled.
Changing a template's field layout changes the fields shown on every test case using it, across every linked project. Say how many projects are affected before writing.
Creating, editing and deleting templates are paid-plan features; on a free plan the call reports failure in the body while still answering 200, and reading templates stays available.

The Review & Approve system fields (reviewers and review status) are hidden from reads on this surface and re-added automatically whenever the property fields are rewritten, so they can be neither seen nor removed here.
A template only affects a project once it is linked to it; creating a template links it to nothing unless linkage is requested.
Failures arrive as a single human-readable message next to a false success flag rather than as a structured error code.

Only test-case and test-result templates can be listed through the older settings surface. Asking it for test-plan or exploratory-session templates fails outright rather than returning an empty list, and the kind must always be stated — there is no default.
Only test-case templates exist today; there are no templates for runs, plans or results, so every template's entity reads TestCase.

A template's step style is fixed at creation: classic step rows or Gherkin (feature, background, scenario). A case authored on a Gherkin template cannot take step rows and vice versa, so choose the template before writing steps.

Templates belong to the workspace but apply only in the projects they are linked to. Naming a template that is unknown to, or not visible from, the caller's workspace is refused outright rather than falling back to the default.
Exactly one template is the default; a case created without naming a template lands on it. System templates ship with the workspace and cannot be deleted.
Disabled templates still appear in the listing (enabled false) but should not be offered for new cases.
Creating, editing, cloning, linking and deleting templates are paid-plan operations and are not exposed through these capabilities; only listing is.

test_case.title: Test case
test_case.description: The unit of test logic: title, preconditions, steps and expected results.
key_facts: A filter is a (key, value) pair and each half fails silently: an unknown KEY is dropped (you get the whole project with success: true), and a wrong-form VALUE matches nothing (count: 0, also success: true). So resolve both — never guess either — and see pagination-and-filtering for the key table and each value's source.

A surprising count means check the FORM, not try another value: 0 on a value the user plainly meant = wrong form, so go resolve ids; filtered count == unfiltered count = the key was dropped. Never take either count from a per_page: 1 call — it returns count: 1 regardless of the real total.
required.fields ADDS joined columns; it does NOT slim a row, so naming fields never buys more rows per page. required.fields=["count"] ALONE is the only value that changes the response.

The compact response has a DIFFERENT envelope: no `success` key ({test_cases, info, filter_details} only — absence of success is NOT failure), info.page_size echoes the server ceiling not your per_page, and filter_details is {} so confirm filter intent before the call.

READING ROWS to show a user: leave per_page at its default and walk p until info.next is null. p advances by per_page and not by what came back, so paging over an incomplete read never recovers the gap.
Paths take INTEGER ids (project + folder + case). The case's TC-NNN comes back as data.test_case.identifier on any read; folder ids are plain integers.
Every successful edit to a test case writes a new version, and an earlier version can be restored — so an edit is recoverable even though nothing offers an undo. Deleting the case is not.

That safety net is plan-gated: below an Enterprise or Team-Pro plan only the last 30 days of versions are visible, and restoring one needs a paid plan — so an older edit may not be recoverable in practice.

The newer v2 project surface addresses a test case by its TC-NNN identifier — or by its third-party identifier in workspaces that issue project-level ids — and does not accept the internal integer id; the older v1 surface is the reverse.

Custom fields on a test case are addressed by their display NAME on the v2 surface and by numeric field id on the v1 surface; a name the project does not define is skipped without any error, so a typo reads back as a successful call that changed nothing.

Priority, status and case type are per-project configurable values, not a fixed vocabulary: send the project's own display value (or its numeric id) and resolve the set from the project's system field values before writing.

Priority, status, case type and automation state are per-project configurable option sets. The single-case write paths accept either the numeric option id or the project's display name, but every BULK write requires the numeric id — a display name there is stored as a broken id with no error. Resolve the ids from the project's system field values first.
`status` is the exception on every path, single and bulk alike: it is only ever taken as a numeric option id, never resolved from a display name.

A case's steps are only ever read from `test_case_steps`. A key called `steps` is legacy, is parsed as a JSON-encoded STRING, and turns a real JSON array into an empty step list — wiping the case's steps while still reporting success.

`estimate` is a dead field: it is accepted on the write paths and then never stored, and every read serialises it as null. The estimate that actually persists is `estimated_duration_seconds`, in seconds, and it is not settable through any bulk edit.

Bulk operations switch to a background job above a size threshold that differs per operation — around 30 for a copy, 100 for an edit or move, 300 for a delete or restore. Past it the call returns an acknowledgement with a unique id instead of the result, so anything that reads the response body as the outcome is wrong for large selections.
Two bulk operations cannot touch the same cases at once: the second is refused with a 'TestCases in progress with another operation' error. That is a retry, not bad input.
Archiving and un-archiving test cases, and listing the archive, are gated on a paid plan — and the refusal comes back as a SUCCESSFUL response carrying success:false, not as an error status.

Whether deleting a case is recoverable depends on the workspace: where the Bin is enabled the case is moved there and can be restored, otherwise the delete is permanent. Either way the case's results and schedule links do not come back.

Creating a case from a template is not automatic: when neither a template name nor a step type is sent, the write paths default to the plain-text template, which stores no steps at all and still reports success.

test_plan.title: Test plan (and sub-plan)
test_plan.description: A container grouping several test runs, typically for one release or milestone.
key_facts: Paths take the INTEGER plan id. The prefixed identifier (TP-NNN / STP-NNN) is for display; never put it in a v1 path.
The read detail has NO data wrapper: the plan sits under a top-level test_plan key, and test_plan.identifier is the TP-NNN / STP-NNN.
Sub-plans are HIDDEN by default in the list. Without include_sub_plans=true you see only top-level plans, so a sub-plan the user named will look missing.

name IS REQUIRED ON EVERY PLAN UPDATE, including one that only touches test_runs. Omit it and the call is rejected with 400 {success: false, error: 'Invalid Update Params'} however valid the rest of the body is — the server's edit branch is gated on name being present. Read the plan first and echo its current name back unchanged. Only a pure plan_status transition and a reviewers-only edit are exempt. Verified live: {test_plan: {test_runs: [198]}} 400s; adding name makes the identical call succeed.

Run ids in test_runs are the INTEGER uuid from a run read — NOT the run's id field, which is the TR-NNN string on every run endpoint (list, plan's run list, single detail alike). Identifiers are forwarded to the backing service uncoerced and fail upstream (observed 502 Upstream service error). Take uuid, never id.

Linking a run MOVES it: a run belongs to at most one plan, so linking silently unlinks it from the plan that held it, with nothing in the 200 to say so. Read the runs' current membership first and tell the user which plans will lose runs. Verified live.

test_runs accepts an id array OR a bulk-selection object {select_all, de_selected_ids, search_query}. select_all means 'the newest active runs', NOT 'everything matching' — and `filters` is accepted but SILENTLY IGNORED, so a filtered select_all links the whole recent set. Narrow with search_query (name/identifier substring) or send explicit ids. Verified live.
bulk-archive / bulk-retrieve go ASYNC above the bulk threshold and return {success, async: true, unique_id} — the plans are NOT changed yet. Re-read to confirm; see async-jobs.
execution-trend is scoped by EXACTLY ONE of test_plan_id / test_run_id. Both → 400 'Provide either test_plan_id or test_run_id, not both'; neither → 400 'test_plan_id or test_run_id is required'.
execution-trend and linked-sessions-chart-data return chart DATA. There is no insights-widget object to create, update, or delete in this profile.

A plan's status only moves forward, one step at a time: new -> started -> completed. Once completed the plan is FROZEN — even a rename is refused with 'Cannot update completed test plan' — so complete it last.
Plans keep no version history. An overwritten name, description or date is gone for good; there is no prior revision to restore, unlike a test case.

The same plan is addressed two different ways depending on which generation of the API you are on: the newer surface takes the prefixed identifier (TP-NNN / STP-NNN), the older one the numeric id. Carry whichever the capability you picked declares.

On the newer surface a run's plan membership is changed from the RUN, never from the plan: the plan's own edit ignores a list of runs entirely (the older surface accepts one). Linking still moves the run out of whatever plan held it.
On the newer surface a sub-plan's parent is fixed when it is created — there is no re-parenting or promotion to a top-level plan there, and the plan's owner is always whoever created it.

Creating a plan takes a name and nothing else; a name is mandatory on create, on clone, and on almost every edit. A status supplied at creation time is accepted and then ignored — a new plan always starts in the `new` state.

A status change and a content edit cannot travel together: when a request moves the plan's status, everything else it carries (name, description, tags, issues, owner) is silently dropped. Rename first, then move the status.
Starting a plan needs its start date in the same request and completing it needs its end date; the dates already stored on the plan are not used as a fallback.

Archiving is an optional feature for the account. When it is switched off, every archive, restore and archived read answers as though the address did not exist — that is a feature gap, not a missing plan.
Reading or restoring archived plans requires the same permission as DELETING a plan, so someone who can happily create and edit plans may still be refused the archived view.
Archived plans vanish from the normal plan listing entirely and have their own listing and their own count; archived sub-plans appear in neither.
An archived plan reads as missing unless the read explicitly opts in to archived records.

Cloning a plan is a background job: the reply confirms the job was queued and carries no id, name or identifier for the copy, and nothing except the runs and sub-plans is inherited — the new plan's description, dates, tags and owner all come from the clone request.

Owner is given as the person's test-management user id, not their BrowserStack id or email, and an id that does not resolve inside the account is discarded rather than rejected — leaving the plan with no owner.
Tags are all-or-nothing: if any entry in the list is not a plain string the entire tag list is dropped without an error.

test_run.title: Test run
test_run.description: One execution cycle over a fixed set of test cases.
key_facts: Only test_case_ids / selection / shared_selection put cases in a run. `filters` and `dynamic_filter` are a forward-sync rule, NOT a selection: a create carrying only `filters` returns 200 with ZERO cases, and sets is_dynamic: true even though you did not ask. Verified live.

Dynamic runs match on nine fields only: priority, status, category, owner, automation_status, automation_state, folder, tags, issues. created_at/updated_at are stored and echoed on read but NEVER matched, so a 'last 7 days' dynamic run drops the date window and over-collects forever. Create runs static unless the user explicitly asks for sync.

test_run.run_state is MANDATORY on create and edit (new_run | in_progress | under_review | rejected | done | closed). It is validated before the selection, so a bare 400 'invalid data' means a bad test_run field — NOT a bad selection shape.

A run's `id` FIELD is the TR-NNN STRING, not the integer — on the project list, a plan's linked-run list and the single-run detail alike. The integer lives in `uuid` ({id: 'TR-90', uuid: 198}). Paths tolerate either form, which hides this; bodies and UI paths do not. Carrying `id` into a test plan's test_runs array sends a string that reaches the backing service uncoerced and 502s there. Take `uuid` whenever a run id leaves a read.
Full lifecycle is exposed: create, edit, assign, bulk-assign cases, bulk-edit results, clone, close, delete.
A test run keeps NO version history and has no restore: unlike a test case, an edited name, cleared tag list or removed case cannot be recovered. Confirm before overwriting or removing.
Removing a case from a run deletes the results recorded against it unless the caller explicitly asks to preserve them — the default is to discard.

Changing which cases a run covers is always queued: the call returns an acceptance immediately and the run still shows the old case list for a moment. Re-read the run's cases to confirm, and do not retry on the acceptance.
Every way of editing a run only ever ADDS cases to it. Taking cases out is a separate operation, and only that one can shrink a run.
The newer API generation identifies a run and its project only by their prefixed ids (TR-14, PR-1) and rejects the plain integers the older generation still tolerates.

Listing a project's runs hides closed ones by default. Unless the caller asks to include closed runs, or filters on a lifecycle state, a run count or 'all our runs' answer silently omits every closed run and still looks complete.

Filtering a run listing by owner fails open: an email that matches nobody in the group is dropped from the filter rather than refused, so a misspelled name returns a wider list that reads as a correct answer. Filtering by plan or by date fails closed and errors instead.

Creating a run does not populate it synchronously. The run exists as soon as the call succeeds, but its test cases are attached by background work, so an immediate read of the run's cases can come back empty or short. Re-read rather than retrying the create, which makes a second run.
A run's name is optional at creation: leave it out and the run is named 'Test Run' plus today's date, which is how projects end up with several identically named runs.

Marking a run as an automation run is not something a caller can do at creation — the flag is accepted and discarded, but it still decides which permission is demanded, so asking for it can be refused outright.

Rows in a run are per case-and-configuration pair, not per test case: a case covered by three configurations is three rows with the same case id and three different mapping ids. Every bulk operation on a run addresses those mapping ids, and passing the test case's own id instead returns success and changes nothing.

Cloning a run copies NO test cases unless the caller explicitly asks for them. A clone requested without a case selection succeeds and produces an empty run, and the clone always starts in the new-run state with no configurations, owner or sync rule carried over.

Bulk changes inside a run switch from immediate to queued above 300 selected rows, and the queued form returns an acknowledgement with no data. The selected rows are locked while either form runs, so a second bulk operation touching any of them is refused as contention rather than queued behind it.
Deleting a finished run needs a different permission from deleting one still in progress, so a role that can clear up working runs can be refused on completed ones.

Discovering how many cases a selection really covers is a distinct read: it multiplies the cases by the configurations, so the number it returns is routinely far larger than the number of cases chosen.

Editing a run requires resending its lifecycle state on every call, including edits that only change the name. A rejected edit that reports nothing more than 'invalid data' is almost always that missing state, not a bad case selection.

user.title: User
user.description: A member with access to a project: who you assign a case to, or set as an owner.
key_facts: WRITE BODIES take the integer: test_case.owner, test_run.owner/assignee_id — send 14.
An unrecognised q key is dropped, not rejected — the server silently omits that condition and returns an unfiltered set that looks like a successful filter. Use the documented key names verbatim.

Every person has two ids: a Test Management user id and a BrowserStack account id. Owner and assignee fields take the Test Management id; several listing filters take the BrowserStack one instead. Sending the wrong one usually matches nobody rather than failing, so check which the operation wants.
Both user reads here are scoped to the whole workspace, not to a project — neither can answer 'who has access to this project', and one of them says so in its path while doing the opposite.
Name search matches the full name only; there is no partial-email search. An exact-email lookup exists and returns at most one person.
Only active users are listed, so someone who has left the workspace cannot be resolved even when their name is still on a case or run.

An unrecognised search key is dropped rather than rejected — the condition silently disappears and an unfiltered set comes back looking like a successful filter. Use the documented key names verbatim.

version.title: Test case version
version.description: A point-in-time snapshot of a test case, for viewing or restoring an earlier revision.
key_facts: Each record carries source (create/update), modified_fields, a modified map (per-field old/new), user and created_at.
diff (compare two versions) and restore require a PAID plan; listing + single-version reads work otherwise. Degrade gracefully.
A plain-language diff summary is agent-side — read the field deltas and describe them; the API returns structured data, not prose.

A revision is addressed two different ways depending on the generation of the read: the older listing hands back a numeric history record id, the newer one identifies a revision only by its position label V1, V2, … with V1 the oldest revision still visible.

Without an Enterprise or Team Pro plan only the last 30 days of a test case's revisions are visible; older ones are absent with no flag saying so, and position labels count only what is visible, so they renumber as old revisions age out.
In the newer payload the editor arrives as updated_by, an email string that is null when the user cannot be resolved in this group, instead of the nested user object the older records carry.

A revision listing populates the per-field old/new detail only for the FIRST record on each page; every other record names the changed fields but not their values, so summarising a page of changes costs one extra read per revision.

Comparing two revisions only looks at a fixed set of fields (name, description, preconditions, automation status, type, status, priority, owner, assignee, folder, tags, defects, custom fields, steps, attachments, reviewers, review status). A change to anything else is invisible in a comparison.

Restoring is a full overwrite of the snapshotted fields, not a merge: a custom field that is empty in the snapshot is cleared, steps added since are removed, and attachments added since are unlinked. Say what will be lost before restoring.
A restore is applied as an ordinary edit, so the pre-restore state stays in the revision trail and can itself be restored — that is the only way back, and there is no undo action.

comment.title: Comment
comment.description: A rich-text note a team member posts on a test case, on its execution in a test run, or on a test plan, to discuss it.
comment.id_convention: Plain integer, assigned on creation and returned as `id` on the posted comment. Existing comment ids are not guessable and must be discovered through the comment listing.

relations.via: scoped to the case's execution in

key_facts: A comment can hang off a test case in its folder, off a test case's execution inside a specific test run, or off a test plan. Only the test-run variant is published in this pass; folder-scoped test-case comments and test-plan comments exist in the product but are not exposed here.

Comments are a paid-plan feature. On a free plan every comment call comes back HTTP 200 with success:false and the message 'This Feature is only for paid customers' — the body, not the status, carries the refusal.
Reading and posting comments both need the test-case VIEW permission; no separate comment or write permission exists, so anyone who can see the case can comment on it.
Comments cannot be posted on automation test runs (Automate/Observability-backed), and not on an archived test case; reading an archived case's comments still works.

Mentioning a colleague — via the mention span markup carrying their BrowserStack user id — notifies them immediately, and the run owner is alerted on every new comment. A mention of someone outside the group fails the whole post.
The body is HTML rich text. Whitespace-only or tag-only content is refused; an inline image counts as content. Stored HTML can differ from what was sent (links normalised, mentions rewritten).
Threads are per run/case/configuration cell: a case mapped to three configurations in a run has three separate comment threads, chosen by the mapping id.
Listings come newest first, 30 to a batch, and the size cannot be changed. Asking beyond the end returns the last batch again rather than an empty one, so stop when the next-batch marker is null.
Posting a comment is recoverable: the author can edit it or delete it afterwards, and deletion hides the comment rather than destroying it. Neither edit nor delete is exposed in this pass.

On each returned comment `edited` is true once it has been changed after posting; the author object's `id` is the internal TM user id (not the BrowserStack user id) and is null for imported comments, which show the original author's name instead.

Mentioning a colleague in a comment notifies them straight away, and the owner of the item commented on is notified of every new comment. Both are real messages that leave the product and cannot be recalled.
A person can only be mentioned if they belong to the same account; naming anyone else is refused rather than quietly ignored.

Only the person who wrote a comment can edit or delete it. Editing replaces the earlier text and keeps no previous version, and a deleted comment disappears from every listing with no self-serve way to restore it.
Comments are stored as rich text, so formatting, links and images survive, and a mention is stored as markup that displays as the person's name.
New comments cannot be added to an archived test case, although the comments already on it stay readable.
Comments are flat - each one sits on the item itself, and there is no way to reply beneath another comment.
Commenting is a paid-plan feature; on a plan without it the answer reports the feature as unavailable instead of failing.

issue.title: Linked issue
issue.description: A ticket in an external tracker such as Jira that test cases and runs are linked to.
issue.id_convention: The external tracker's own ticket key, as a string — for Jira an uppercase project key, a hyphen and digits, e.g. PROJ-123; other trackers use their own form. It is never a Test Management integer id and cannot be minted here: take it from the tracker itself, or read it from the linked-ticket list carried on a test case or test run. Test Management does not validate that the key exists, so a wrong key links silently.
key_facts: A linked issue is not stored by Test Management — only the link is. Unlinking removes the association and leaves the test case, the test run and the tracker ticket untouched, so every unlink here is reversible by linking again.
Linking and unlinking never write anything back into the external tracker; the ticket is not commented on, transitioned or modified.
One ticket can carry many test cases and many test runs, and one test case can be linked to several tickets, including tickets in different trackers.
The tracker a link belongs to is part of its identity: the same ticket key recorded under two different trackers is two independent links.
Unlinking identifies the link by the test case or test run plus the tracker, not by the ticket, so a case linked to several tickets in one tracker cannot be unlinked from a chosen one.
Test Management also has a separate Requirements feature of its own; a linked issue always lives in an external tracker and is a different thing, even though customers call both 'requirements'.
Ticket keys are never checked against the tracker, so a mistyped key produces a link to a ticket that does not exist and reports success.

shared_field.title: Shared field
shared_field.description: A reusable block of test content that many test cases embed, kept in collections.
shared_field.id_convention: Plain integer, not guessable; discover ids by listing a project's shared fields. A shared step id comes from a different set and will not resolve as a shared field.
key_facts: A shared field is not a shared step. They are separate objects with separate listings and separate ids, and they are easy to confuse because both are reusable content - establish which one the user means before acting on an id.
The API calls this object a shared component while the product calls it a shared field; they are the same thing under two names.
Every shared field has a type - step, background or precondition - and the type decides where a test case can embed it.
Shared fields are organised into collections, which nest. A field placed in no collection sits in the Unassigned root.
A shared field is embedded by many test cases at once, so editing or deleting one changes every case that uses it; the usage count on the field is the measure of that blast radius.
